Factored One-sided Adam-Moment
for Practical and Scalable SOAP

Jaemyung Yu⋆    Byeongho Heo    Sangdoo Yun    Dongyoon Han⋆ Affiliation: NAVER AI Lab
Abstract

Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and we measure only a 15–20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP’s optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP’s gains need not require SOAP’s cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam.

1 Introduction

Adam [23] and AdamW [32] have long been the default for pre-training transformer architectures, including large language models (LLMs). Their successors, including memory-efficient adaptive optimizers [50, 51, 53, 15], show that comparable optimization quality can be achieved with substantially less optimizer memory. In another direction, Shampoo [16], a foundational method in the family of Kronecker-factored second-order optimizers, has shown that the optimization quality of adaptive first-order methods such as Adam can be surpassed. Its most practical variant, SOAP [44], the Adam-in-eigenbasis version of Shampoo, reports 35–40% improvements in wall-clock time and step count over AdamW at large batch sizes, building upon the Distributed Shampoo baselines [3, 40] that won the external-tuning track of the first AlgoPerf competition [6, 21].

Still, practitioners often default to AdamW or Muon [20], because SOAP achieves its gains at the expense of computational efficiency, requiring about 4.5×4.5{\times} the optimizer state of AdamW and a significantly slower per-step wall-clock time. More specifically, SOAP’s memory is dominated by the first moment, the second moment in the eigenbasis-rotated space, and the two Kronecker factor matrices L=G​G⊤L=GG^{\top} (m2m^{2}) and R=G⊤​GR=G^{\top}G (n2n^{2}) of a gradient G∈ℝm×nG\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. Its runtime is further occupied by the periodic eigendecomposition of these factor matrices, which makes SOAP substantially more expensive than AdamW despite its strong optimization performance.

This paper aims to retain SOAP-level quality while approaching AdamW-level cost. Our motivation is simple. If SOAP’s computational overhead can be sufficiently reduced, its optimization advantages could make it a practical successor to AdamW. To this end, we revisit SOAP’s major cost components and show that several can be relaxed or replaced without sacrificing performance. The original SOAP paper [44] already evaluated one-sided and factored variants, but as cost-reducing ablations without a criterion for when they preserve quality. Frans et al. [12] then found that input-only rotation and a factored variance each retain most of SOAP’s quality, and other works [30, 11] improved SOAP along other axes. Our contribution is thus not one-sided preconditioning or factorization itself, but explaining which side to retain, when factorization is justified, and why their combination is effective.

Concretely, our approach is built on two structural simplifications: input-only preconditioning and a factored Adam-Moment update. The first simplification drops the output-side factor LL and retains only the input-side factor RR, eliminating its m2m^{2} memory and one of the two eigendecompositions. Its justification follows from the Kronecker structure of the Hessian, in which all output rows of an affine layer share the same input-side outer product x​x⊤xx^{\top} [25], while the Hessian of transformer layers is empirically near-block-diagonal along output neurons or heads [50], making the input-only form the natural one-sided approximation. The second simplification replaces the dense rotated second moment with a row-and-column factored estimator, r∈ℝmr\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and c∈ℝnc\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, with trace normalization, reducing the buffer size from m​nmn to m+nm+n. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption [35] with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and the K-FAC part holds to a 1515–20%20\% relative error in practice. Together, these simplifications reduce SOAP’s optimizer state from 2​m​n+2​m2+2​n22mn+2m^{2}+2n^{2} to m​n+2​n2+m+nmn+2n^{2}+m+n and the amortized eigendecomposition count from two to one. We call the resulting method FOAM (Factored One-sided Adam-Moment).

Figure 1 highlights FOAM’s main advantages. On pre-training, FOAM matches the strong Muon and SOAP baselines on validation loss with half of SOAP’s optimizer state and reaches AdamW’s final loss within 7%7\% of AdamW’s own wall-clock time, while SOAP needs more than twice as long at 760M, and FOAM matches AdamW’s hyperparameter robustness over a three-fold learning-rate range. The advantage holds from 124M to 760M parameters with learning rates re-tuned at every size from a μ\muP [46] anchor. In summary, our contributions are: (i) a structural justification of input-only preconditioning, with the Kronecker structure of the Hessian and empirical verifications with LLMs with recent architectural elements; (ii) a factored Adam-Moment update with trace normalization, exact under K-FAC with a diagonal output curvature and empirically validated through K-FAC-residual measurements during training; and (iii) the resulting algorithm FOAM, a scalable and practical SOAP variant that delivers SOAP-class quality with half of SOAP’s optimizer state (+7.4%+7.4\% measured peak training memory over AdamW) and Muon-class wall-clock time.

2 Related Work

Adaptive optimizers can be categorized by how aggressively they approximate the empirical Fisher F=𝔼⁡[vec⁡(G)​vec​(G)⊤]F=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{vec}(G)\,\mathrm{vec}(G)^{\top}], which all of Adam [23]/AdamW [32], Shampoo [16], and SOAP [44] implicitly use as a curvature surrogate in place of the true Fisher [24].

2.1 Empirical Fisher and Kronecker-factored Optimizers

AdaGrad [8] introduced per-coordinate scaling by an empirical second-moment statistic, an early diagonal approximation of the inverse empirical Fisher. K-FAC [35] replaces the diagonal with a Kronecker product, F≈𝔼⁡[a​a⊤]⊗𝔼⁡[s​s⊤]F\approx\mathbb{E}[aa^{\top}]\otimes\mathbb{E}[ss^{\top}] where aa is the layer input and ss the gradient with respect to the layer’s pre-activation output, the assumption under which our factored Adam-Moment update is exact. Eschenhagen et al. [10] adapt K-FAC to transformer architectures via the expand and reduce flavors. Shampoo [16] carries this idea to the matrix parameters. It maintains EMAs of L=G​G⊤L=GG^{\top} and R=G⊤​GR=G^{\top}G and steps in L−1/4GR−1/4L^{-1/4}GR^{-1/4}, i.e., it preconditions by (R⊗L)−1/4(R\otimes L)^{-1/4}; Morwani et al. [36] show that R⊗LR\otimes L equals one power-iteration step toward the optimal Kronecker-product approximation of the empirical Fisher and is empirically close to it. SOAP [44] eigendecomposes LL and RR and runs Adam in the resulting rotated coordinates, an EKFAC-style construction [14] that Lu et al. [33] interpret as gradient whitening. Variants modify specific pieces: CASPR [9] combines the per-axis factors through a Kronecker sum instead of a Kronecker product. KL-Shampoo and KL-SOAP [30] recast the family via KL-divergence minimization, and Purifying Shampoo [11] shows that trace scaling of the preconditioner can replace learning-rate grafting, which corroborates our trace-norm choice in §4.2. The one-sided fallback in distributed Shampoo [3] drops a factor on memory grounds, whereas we give a structural argument for keeping the input side (§4.1). Purifying Shampoo’s adaptive tolerance criterion for skipping the periodic eigendecomposition is adopted unchanged as FOAM’s amortized eigenbasis-refresh policy (§4.2).

2.2 Optimizers with Coarser Approximations

A second line of work adopts coarser approximations to the empirical Fisher in exchange for lower computational cost. Adam [23, 32] keeps only the diagonal of FF, sacrificing all matrix structure. Signum [4] keeps only the sign of the momentum. Muon [20] replaces the second-moment buffer with Newton-Schulz orthogonalization M(M⊤M)−1/2M(M^{\top}M)^{-1/2}, which can be read as a square-root natural-gradient step under a structured Fisher R~⊗Im\tilde{R}\otimes I_{m} with an input-side factor R~∈ℝn×n\tilde{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} shared across output rows [34, 15]. AdaMuon [41] adds an element-wise Adam-style second moment on top of the orthogonalized update. SPlus [13], a related SOAP variant, replaces the rotated second moment with sign normalization in the Shampoo eigenbasis and adds iterate averaging. Recent Muon variants (NorMuon [28], Muon2 [31], NAMO [48], Polar Express [2]) refine specific components of Muon. A parallel branch targets memory-efficient AdamW rather than matching SOAP-class quality: Adam-mini [50], GaLore [51], APOLLO [53], Alice [15], and SWAN [34]. We exclude these methods from the main comparison since they mainly target a smaller memory footprint than AdamW, whereas we target SOAP-level performance at near-Adam cost.

Positioning our method. FOAM lies at the intersection of these two branches. It stays within the Kronecker-factored Fisher framework but borrows the factored-second-moment idea from Adafactor [39]’s row-by-column estimator, applied here in the rotated coordinates of SOAP. Both ingredients appear in the SOAP paper as cost-reducing ablations, a one-sided variant and an Adafactor-style factored second moment in the eigenbasis, and Frans et al. [12] found empirically that input-only rotation and a factored variance each preserve most of SOAP’s quality; the distinction lies in the criteria. SOAP’s one-sided variant keeps the side with the smaller dimension, whereas we keep the input side irrespective of size (§4.1), so the two rules choose opposite sides for the MLP down-projection; likewise, we factorize only after the input-side rotation, which makes the rotated second moment separable into row and column factors (Lemma 1, §4.2).

3 Preliminary: Shampoo and SOAP

We consider a transformer with matrix parameters W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, where nn and mm denote the input and output dimensions, respectively. Let Gt∈ℝm×nG_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} denote the mini-batch gradient at step tt. Following the convention of SOAP [44], we define the two Kronecker factors LtL_{t} and RtR_{t} as the second-moment matrices of the gradient:

Lt=𝔼⁡[Gt​Gt⊤]∈ℝm×m,Rt=𝔼⁡[Gt⊤​Gt]∈ℝn×n,L_{t}\;=\;\mathbb{E}[G_{t}G_{t}^{\top}]\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{m\times m},\qquad R_{t}\;=\;\mathbb{E}[G_{t}^{\top}G_{t}]\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, (1)

LtL_{t} acts on the left side (output) of GtG_{t}, and RtR_{t} acts on the right side (input). In practice, both are estimated by exponential moving averages (EMAs), for which we reuse the same symbols, and we reserve the term estimator for such EMA buffers. Shampoo [16] takes a fractional inverse of each factor and applies the preconditioned update:

Wt+1=Wt−ηLt−1/4GtRt−1/4,W_{t+1}\;=\;W_{t}\;-\;\eta\,L_{t}^{-1/4}\,G_{t}\,R_{t}^{-1/4}, (2)

with learning rate η\eta. SOAP [44] instead eigendecomposes LtL_{t} and RtR_{t} to obtain orthogonal rotations QL∈ℝm×mQ_{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} and QR∈ℝn×nQ_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, and runs Adam in the rotated coordinates:

Grot=QL⊤​G​QR∈ℝm×n,G_{\rm rot}\;=\;Q_{L}^{\top}\,G\,Q_{R}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, (3)

following the EKFAC tradition [14] that tracks diagonal second moments in the eigenbasis of a Kronecker-factored preconditioner. The per-step update maintains a dense second moment vrot∈ℝm×nv_{\rm rot}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} in the rotated space. The rotations QLQ_{L} and QRQ_{R} are refreshed every 𝚙𝚏\mathtt{pf} (precondition frequency) steps via two eigendecompositions of LtL_{t} and RtR_{t}. LtL_{t} and RtR_{t} require m2+n2m^{2}+n^{2} memory, the rotated second moment vrotv_{\rm rot} requires an additional m​nmn memory, and the periodic eigendecompositions incur further computational overhead. These costs constitute the overhead structure that FOAM addresses.

4 Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM)

We propose FOAM, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment, which combines two structural simplifications of SOAP into a single optimizer. FOAM applies an input-side K-FAC factor combined with a factored output diagonal. It maintains only the input-side factor RtR_{t}, runs Adam in the eigenbasis QR=eigh⁡(Rt)Q_{R}=\mathrm{eigh}(R_{t}), and replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment vrot∈ℝm×nv_{\rm rot}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with a row-column factored estimator v^rot=τ​r^​c^⊤\hat{v}_{\rm rot}=\tau\,\hat{r}\,\hat{c}^{\top}. Here r^∈ℝm\hat{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and c^∈ℝn\hat{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} are bias-corrected EMAs of the row and column means of the squared rotated gradient, and τ\tau is a trace-matching scalar. The two simplifications together give FOAM the implicit Fisher Rt⊗diag⁡(r^t)R_{t}\otimes\mathrm{diag}(\hat{r}_{t}), a full input-side factor with a diagonal output side, derived in Algorithm 1 and the following sections. Figure 2 compares this preconditioner structure with those of Adam, Muon, and SOAP against the near-block-diagonal Hessian of a transformer layer, where FOAM keeps SOAP’s input factor with a diagonal output side.

Derivation overview. The steps below form a single chain from 𝔼⁡[g​g⊤]\mathbb{E}[gg^{\top}], g=vec⁡(G)g=\mathrm{vec}(G), to the two stored vectors. (i) Under K-FAC, 𝔼⁡[g​g⊤]=R⊗L\mathbb{E}[gg^{\top}]=R\otimes L, and LL is near-diagonal (§4.1), so the off-diagonal structure lives on the input side, which is the side to keep. (ii) Rotating by QRQ_{R} turns the covariance into ΛR⊗L\Lambda_{R}\otimes L (Lemma 1). Like SOAP running Adam in its eigenbasis, FOAM keeps only the diagonal of this covariance, a modeling choice that the rotation makes accurate. (iii) This diagonal, reshaped to m×nm\times n, is the rank-one matrix diag⁡(L)​λR⊤\mathrm{diag}(L)\,\lambda_{R}^{\top}, so storing r^\hat{r} and c^\hat{c} keeps every coordinate’s own variance and loses nothing relative to the dense m​nmn buffer, as formalized in §4.2.

4.1 Input-only Preconditioning

Our idea is to remove the output-side factor LtL_{t} and maintain only Rt←β2​Rt−1+(1−β2)​Gt⊤​GtR_{t}\leftarrow\beta_{2}R_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{2})\,G_{t}^{\top}G_{t} with its eigenbasis QR=eigh⁡(Rt)Q_{R}=\mathrm{eigh}(R_{t}). The gradient rotation is applied only to the input axis, i.e., Grot=G​QR∈ℝm×nG_{\rm rot}=G\,Q_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. This reduces the factor-state memory from 𝒪⁡(m2+n2)\mathcal{O}(m^{2}+n^{2}) to 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) and the number of eigendecompositions from two to one, halving this cost for square matrices.

A conceptual justification comes from the curvature of an affine layer with cross-entropy loss, the standard loss for language modeling and classification. For y=W​xy=Wx and p=softmax⁡(y)p=\mathrm{softmax}(y), the Hessian of the loss ℓ=−log⁡pk⋆\ell=-\log p_{k^{\star}} for a target class k⋆k^{\star} with respect to WW decomposes exactly as

H=x​x⊤⊗(diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤).H\,=\,xx^{\top}\otimes\big(\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}\big). (4)

The output-side factor diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^{\top} has diagonal entries pi​(1−pi)p_{i}(1-p_{i}) and off-diagonal entries −pi​pk-p_{i}p_{k}. Each off-diagonal entry pi​pkp_{i}p_{k} is smaller than the diagonal entry pi​(1−pi)p_{i}(1-p_{i}) by a factor of pk/(1−pi)p_{k}/(1-p_{i}), which is small for most classes of a large vocabulary even far from a one-hot prediction, in line with the dominant per-class diagonal blocks of softmax linear models [25]. Larger entries arise only where a class takes much of the mass, and each pair (i,k)(i,k) receives them only from examples in which ii or kk is such a class, whereas the diagonal accumulates over all examples, so with a large vocabulary the expected output-side curvature is dominated by its diagonal, and under the K-FAC independence approximation the batch expectation becomes

𝔼⁡[H]≈𝔼⁡[x​x⊤]⊗diag⁡(κ),κi=𝔼⁡[pi​(1−pi)].\mathbb{E}[H]\;\approx\;\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}]\otimes\mathrm{diag}(\kappa),\qquad\kappa_{i}\;=\;\mathbb{E}\big[p_{i}(1-p_{i})\big]. (5)

This has the structure of FOAM’s implicit Fisher, with the input-side curvature 𝔼⁡[x​x⊤]\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}] tracked by RtR_{t} and the per-output curvature scale κi\kappa_{i} absorbed into r^t\hat{r}_{t}. The output side need not be homogeneous across rows. FOAM only requires that it is dominated by its diagonal, which this mechanism suggests and the Gauss-Newton measurements of §5.4 support empirically.

Beyond the affine setting. For a hidden affine layer h=W​xh=Wx, the per-example Hessian keeps the same form x​x⊤⊗∇h2ℓxx^{\top}\otimes\nabla_{h}^{2}\ell, since hh is linear in WW, and only the output-side factor changes, from diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^{\top} to the curvature with respect to hh. The vanishing-off-diagonal mechanism is specific to the output layer, but near-block-diagonal Hessians have been observed in MLPs throughout training [5, 50] and, with blocks along output neurons or heads, in a small transformer [50]. We provide additional indirect evidence specific to our setting through Gauss-Newton alignment measurements in §5.4.

4.2 Factored Eigenvalue Under Input-only Preconditioning

Even with the input-only simplification, SOAP still has overheads due to the dense rotated second-moment buffer vrot∈ℝm×nv_{\rm rot}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. Our next step is to replace it with two factored estimators r∈ℝmr\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and c∈ℝnc\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, EMAs of the row- and column-means of Grot∘2=Grot∘GrotG_{\rm rot}^{\circ 2}=G_{\rm rot}\circ G_{\rm rot}, and reconstruct the rotated second moment as an outer product with trace normalization:

v^rot​[i,j]=τ⋅r^​[i]⋅c^​[j],τ=tr⁡(R)‖r^‖1​‖c^‖1.\hat{v}_{\rm rot}[i,j]\;=\;\tau\cdot\hat{r}[i]\cdot\hat{c}[j],\qquad\tau\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{tr}(R)}{\|\hat{r}\|_{1}\,\|\hat{c}\|_{1}}. (6)

The state shrinks from m​nmn to m+nm+n per matrix parameter. The trace-matching scalar τ\tau makes the entries of v^rot\hat{v}_{\rm rot} sum to tr⁡(R)\mathrm{tr}(R), fixing the overall scale of the reconstructed second moment to that of the input-side factor. We now justify why this rank-one factorization is sufficient.

Lemma 1 (Covariance of the input-rotated gradient).

Let g=vec⁡(G)∈ℝm​ng=\mathrm{vec}(G)\in\mathbb{R}^{mn} and assume the K-FAC factorization 𝔼⁡[g​g⊤]=R⊗L\mathbb{E}[gg^{\top}]=R\otimes L. Let g′=vec⁡(G​QR)g^{\prime}=\mathrm{vec}(G\,Q_{R}) be the input-rotated gradient in column-major form. Then

𝔼⁡[g′​g′⁣⊤]=ΛR⊗L,\mathbb{E}[g^{\prime}\,g^{\prime\top}]\;=\;\Lambda_{R}\otimes L, (7)

where ΛR=QR⊤​R​QR\Lambda_{R}=Q_{R}^{\top}R\,Q_{R} is the diagonal eigenvalue matrix of RR.

Proof.

Using the column-major identity vec⁡(A​G​B)=(B⊤⊗A)​vec​(G)\mathrm{vec}(AGB)=(B^{\top}\otimes A)\,\mathrm{vec}(G) with A=ImA=I_{m} and B=QRB=Q_{R}, we have g′=(QR⊤⊗Im)​gg^{\prime}=(Q_{R}^{\top}\otimes I_{m})\,g. Therefore,

𝔼⁡[g′​g′⁣⊤]=(QR⊤⊗Im)​𝔼​[g​g⊤]​(QR⊗Im)=(QR⊤⊗Im)​(R⊗L)​(QR⊗Im).\mathbb{E}[g^{\prime}\,g^{\prime\top}]\;=\;(Q_{R}^{\top}\otimes I_{m})\,\mathbb{E}[g\,g^{\top}]\,(Q_{R}\otimes I_{m})\;=\;(Q_{R}^{\top}\otimes I_{m})(R\otimes L)(Q_{R}\otimes I_{m}). (8)

The Kronecker mixed-product identity (A⊗B)​(C⊗D)=(A​C)⊗(B​D)(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=(AC)\otimes(BD), applied twice, gives

(QR⊤⊗Im)​(R⊗L)​(QR⊗Im)=(QR⊤​R​QR)⊗(Im​L​Im)=ΛR⊗L.∎(Q_{R}^{\top}\otimes I_{m})(R\otimes L)(Q_{R}\otimes I_{m})\;=\;(Q_{R}^{\top}R\,Q_{R})\otimes(I_{m}\,L\,I_{m})\;=\;\Lambda_{R}\otimes L.\qed (9)

Lemma 1 tells us two things about the rotated gradient. First, the input-side covariance becomes diagonal, because rotating by QRQ_{R} decorrelates the input directions and replaces RR with its eigenvalues ΛR\Lambda_{R}. Second, the output-side factor LL is unchanged, so when LL is diagonal (§4.1) the rotated covariance ΛR⊗L\Lambda_{R}\otimes L is itself diagonal, and its diagonal, the part FOAM keeps, factorizes as

𝔼⁡[(G​QR)​[i,j]2]=λR​[j]⋅L⁡[i,i],\mathbb{E}\big[(G\,Q_{R})[i,j]^{2}\big]\;=\;\lambda_{R}[j]\cdot L[i,i], (10)

with λR​[j]\lambda_{R}[j] the jj-th diagonal entry of ΛR\Lambda_{R}. The right-hand side is a per-row factor depending only on ii times a per-column factor depending only on jj, so the entire m×nm\times n second-moment surface is captured by m+nm+n numbers rather than m​nmn. The row- and column-means of Grot∘2G_{\rm rot}^{\circ 2} are the natural estimators of these two factors, up to a global scalar that the trace normalization τ\tau removes, so τ​r^​c^⊤\tau\,\hat{r}\,\hat{c}^{\top} recovers the dense m​nmn buffer exactly under K-FAC, and SOAP’s two-sided one when LL is also diagonal. In our runs, the K-FAC assumption is violated by a 1515–20%20\% relative error, mostly at the key projection, yet this costs only about 0.0020.002 nats in final validation loss (Table 3, Appendix C).

Amortized eigenbasis update. The eigenbasis QRQ_{R} is refreshed every 𝚙𝚏\mathtt{pf} steps via the adaptive skip rule of Purifying Shampoo [11]. We form B=QR⊤​Rt​QRB=Q_{R}^{\top}R_{t}Q_{R} and skip the eigendecomposition whenever its off-diagonal ratio off⁡(B)=‖B−diag⁡(B)‖F/‖B‖F≤tol\mathrm{off}(B)=\|B-\mathrm{diag}(B)\|_{F}/\|B\|_{F}\leq\mathrm{tol}, keeping the previous QRQ_{R} (tol=0\mathrm{tol}=0 refreshes at every 𝚙𝚏\mathtt{pf}-th step). With a small tol\mathrm{tol}, an eigendecomposition is invoked only when RtR_{t} has drifted from diagonal in the current basis, which becomes rare late in training.

Complexity. Table 1 compares per-parameter optimizer state and compute. SOAP stores 2​m​n+2​m2+2​n22mn+2m^{2}+2n^{2} values for the first and rotated second moments, two factor EMAs, and two eigenbases. FOAM reduces this to m​n+2​n2+(m+n)mn+2n^{2}+(m+n) for one first moment, the estimators r,cr,c, and the factor RR with its eigenbasis QRQ_{R}. Per-step cost is 𝒪⁡(m​n2)\mathcal{O}(mn^{2}) from the rotation G​QRG\,Q_{R}, matching Muon, and the amortized eigendecomposition cost drops from 𝒪⁡(m3+n3)\mathcal{O}(m^{3}+n^{3}) to 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}).

5 Experiment

This section asks whether FOAM matches strong Muon and SOAP baselines in pre-training across scales (§5.2), and whether its design components are well-founded and each contributes (§5.4).

5.1 Experimental Setup

Setup. We pre-train the models following a modern LLM architectural setup (RoPE [42], RMSNorm [47], untied embeddings, MLP with GELU [17], no bias) at three scales following GPT-2 [38]: small (124M), medium (350M), and large (760M), on FineWeb [37] at a 1×1\times Chinchilla compute budget (≈20\approx\!20 tokens per parameter) [19], giving 2.492.49B, 7.107.10B, and 15.4915.49B training tokens over 4,7504{,}750, 13,55013{,}550, and 29,55029{,}550 optimizer steps, respectively, at a fixed batch of 0.50.5M tokens (1k sequence length). All runs use bfloat16 mixed precision on 8×8{\times}H100 (FSDP [52] at medium and large), with cosine decay to 10%10\% of the peak LR after 2%2\% warmup, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, and ε=10−8\varepsilon\!=\!10^{-8}.

Parameter groups. Following the setup of Jordan et al. [20], Frans et al. [12], only the matrix parameters (Q/K/V/O attention projections and MLP linears) are preconditioned by the optimizer under study, while embeddings, the lm-head, and 1D and norm parameters are routed to a fixed AdamW group with LR 10−210^{-2}, β=(0.95,0.95)\beta\!=\!(0.95,0.95), no weight decay on embeddings, and weight decay 10−310^{-3} on the lm-head. Unless noted, all groups use β=(0.95,0.95)\beta\!=\!(0.95,0.95), and SOAP variants use precondition frequency 𝚙𝚏=10\mathtt{pf}=10 with the Purifying-Shampoo skip tolerance tol=0.1\mathrm{tol}=0.1 [11].

Hyperparameter search. At small we run a 5×55{\times}5 LR/WD grid (factor 101/8≈1.3310^{1/8}\!\approx\!1.33 on LR as in Frans et al. [12], and 101/4≈1.7810^{1/4}\!\approx\!1.78 on WD) per optimizer at β=(0.95,0.95)\beta\!=\!(0.95,0.95), re-centering on grid edges, and re-validate the inner 3×33{\times}3 neighborhood over three seeds. For medium and large, dense LR/WD grids are infeasible, so we transfer the small inner LR via a μ\muP [46] (∝1/width\propto\!1/\text{width}) anchor, sweep 55 LR points (factor 101/810^{1/8}) around it with WD held at the small inner optimum, refine the best point with a 3×33{\times}3 LR/WD grid extended at grid edges, and report the selected cell as the per-size point estimate. Validation loss is reported as mean ±\pm std over 1111 seeds at small and medium and 33 seeds at large.

Baselines. The headline comparison spans AdamW [32], Muon [20], AdaMuon [41], SOAP [44] (the bilateral, dense-vv variant), and FOAM (ours) at all three scales. At GPT-2 small we additionally evaluate SPlus [13], Shampoo [16], and the SOAP variants of our construction ablation (§5.4).

5.2 Main Results

Table 2 reports the main pre-training results across three model scales. SOAP attains the lowest validation loss at every scale, with FOAM behind by 0.0040.004, 0.0080.008, and 0.0050.005 nats at small, medium, and large, each within about one seed std. FOAM is ahead of Muon, AdaMuon, and AdamW at every scale. The cost gap to SOAP widens at scale. FOAM uses half of SOAP’s matrix-parameter state at every size, and its measured peak memory at small size is +7.4%+7.4\% over AdamW against +12.9%+12.9\% for SOAP. On wall-clock time, FOAM needs fewer steps than AdamW to reach AdamW’s final loss, which offsets its higher per-step cost: its time to that loss, tAt_{\mathrm{A}}, is within 7%7\% of AdamW’s own at every scale and equal at large (10.5310.53 vs. 10.5510.55 h), whereas SOAP needs 1.35×1.35\times at small and 2.15×2.15\times at large, as its two eigendecompositions grow cubically with width.

5.3 Hyperparameter Robustness

A practical optimizer must also tolerate imprecise tuning. Figure 3 sweeps LR, WD, and β1,β2\beta_{1},\beta_{2} around each optimizer’s inner best on GPT-2 small. FOAM’s bowl shape and width track AdamW and SOAP across all four axes within 0.050.05 nats. The one notable asymmetry is AdamW’s catastrophic collapse to 3.863.86 at β1=0.99\beta_{1}\!=\!0.99, where SOAP and FOAM degrade by only 0.020.02 nats, so FOAM inherits SOAP’s wider safe range on the momentum axis, as panel (c) shows.

5.4 Analysis

We first measure what each FOAM simplification contributes to quality and cost, then ask whether input-only preconditioning is structurally justified on actual GPT-2 layers, and finally whether the factored update stays close to the dense SOAP update in practice.

FOAM-construction ablation. Table 3 ablates, starting from SOAP, the two structural simplifications of FOAM on GPT-2 small, namely input-only preconditioning, which drops the output-side rotation QLQ_{L}, and the factored second moment, which replaces the dense vv with the row and column estimators r,cr,c. Each variant is evaluated at its own best HP cell with 33 seeds. Input-only preconditioning substantially reduces both optimizer state and wall-clock while keeping validation loss within 0.010.01 nats of full SOAP, whereas output-only preconditioning, at the same state, loses about 0.020.02 nats, in line with the input-output asymmetry analyzed below. Factorization further trades a small wall-clock increase for a meaningful reduction in optimizer state with no measurable loss in validation. Stacked, the two simplifications yield FOAM, which retains SOAP’s validation while halving the matrix-parameter optimizer state. The same holds at medium and large, where input-only SOAP and FOAM differ by at most 0.010.01 nats while the factored second moment saves 18%18\% of the state.

Gauss-Newton fit. Figure 5 compares six implicit preconditioners against the per-layer Gauss-Newton matrix HGNH_{\mathrm{GN}} on all 7272 matrix parameters of the 1212-layer GPT-2 small backbone. SOAP’s full bilateral preconditioner is the closest Kronecker approximant of HGNH_{\mathrm{GN}}, about 6×6\times above Adam-diag and 2×2\times above Muon. The asymmetry between input and output rotations is sharp and persistent. Dropping the output-side rotation costs only a quarter of the alignment, so input-only keeps 75%75\% of SOAP-full at 0.380.38, whereas dropping the input-side rotation costs 80%80\% and leaves output-only at 0.100.10. FOAM, which is input-only and factored, tracks SOAP-input-only within 11–2%2\% at every checkpoint, indicating that factoring the eigenvalue tensor preserves nearly all of input-only’s curvature alignment. This asymmetry, in which the input-feature axis carries the dominant curvature structure, is the empirical justification for the input-only recipe used in the main results. It also holds per module, since on the exact layer-wise Gauss-Newton matrix input-only exceeds output-only in all six module types at both 124M and 350M, by 1.5×1.5\times to 11.5×11.5\times (Appendix D).

Factored update validity. Figure 5 reports two diagnostics that explain why the factored variants of Table 3 preserve quality. The rank-11 share in panel (a) is the key diagnostic. In Adam’s raw g2g^{2} basis, VV is only 0.540.54–0.630.63 rank-11 separable and drifts down during training, while in SOAP’s eigenbasis the rotated VV stays near 0.900.90 for the bilateral rotation and 0.840.84 for the input-only rotation of FOAM. The cosine in panel (b) follows accordingly, at about 0.970.97, 0.960.96, and 0.940.94 in the bilateral, input-only, and raw bases. Consequently, factoring the SOAP-rotated VV loses essentially nothing, costing less than 0.0050.005 nats in validation, whereas Adafactor-style factoring [39] of Adam’s raw VV is far less accurate. With the HGNH_{\mathrm{GN}} alignment of Figure 5, this completes FOAM’s rationale, which rotates into the input-side eigenbasis, where VV becomes nearly rank-11 separable, and then factors.

5.5 Beyond the Main Setting

Scale. At GPT-2 XL, with 1.561.56B parameters and 3131B tokens, FOAM and SOAP are within 0.0010.001 nats over three seeds and both ahead of Muon and AdamW, which are the other two optimizers run at this scale (Appendix E). Modality. On ViT-Tiny trained on Tiny-ImageNet, the matrix-preconditioned optimizers beat AdamW by 6.56.5 to 8.58.5 points of top-1 accuracy, with SOAP first and FOAM second, on par with Muon and AdaMuon (Appendix F). Batch size. At a fixed token budget, growing the batch from 0.50.5M to 22M tokens per step raises AdamW’s loss from 3.3703.370 to 3.9563.956 but FOAM’s only from 3.3093.309 to 3.3643.364. FOAM also stays ahead of Muon in final loss at every batch size, and at 22M tokens per step only FOAM reaches AdamW’s 0.50.5M-batch quality. Larger batches thus stay usable with FOAM, which at 22M tokens per step reaches AdamW’s 0.50.5M-batch quality in about a third of its own 0.50.5M-batch wall-clock time (Appendix G).

6 Discussion and Conclusion

Limitations and future work. Our experiments stop at GPT-2 scale, up to 1.56B parameters, so whether FOAM’s advantages hold for frontier-scale pre-training remains the main open question. Our implementation does not yet shard RR and QRQ_{R} across devices, which matters at the ≥7\geq 7B scale, although the layer-wise distributed optimizer of Khona et al. [22] suggests that this is an engineering rather than a fundamental obstacle. The factored update is least accurate at the key projection, whose gradients pass through RoPE and softmax (Appendix C). Finally, the embeddings and the lm-head stay on AdamW because their vocabulary dimension rules out a dense factor on that side, although a FOAM-style factor on their small hidden dimension would be affordable. Extending FOAM to these layers, and attention-aware factorizations for the key projection, are natural next steps.

When to use FOAM. FOAM fits when SOAP-class quality is needed but SOAP’s memory or wall-clock is binding, since it stays within 0.0040.004–0.0080.008 nats of SOAP at half its optimizer state and, at 760M, about half its wall-clock. Against Muon and AdaMuon, quality slightly favors FOAM at every scale and speed is near parity, while AdaMuon keeps less state. Muon and AdaMuon thus remain preferable when optimizer state is the hardest constraint. Against AdamW, FOAM, like other matrix-preconditioned methods, is most valuable at large effective batch, where AdamW degrades (Appendix G) and, at fixed 𝚙𝚏\mathtt{pf}, the optimizer’s compute share shrinks. FOAM is least attractive when memory is dominated by modules with a large input dimension, such as the MLP down-projection, whose n2n^{2} factor carries most of FOAM’s residual state over AdamW.

Conclusion. We presented FOAM, a scalable and practical SOAP variant built on two structural simplifications: input-only preconditioning, justified by the Kronecker structure of the Hessian and a near-diagonal output curvature, and a factored Adam-Moment update, exact under K-FAC, with Purifying Shampoo’s skip rule for the amortized eigenbasis update. Where memory-efficient variants mainly shrink AdamW’s memory, FOAM addresses the complementary problem and brings SOAP-level quality close to Adam-level cost. FOAM matches strong Muon and SOAP baselines on LLM pre-training with modern architectures while using half of SOAP’s optimizer state and Muon-level wall-clock time, from 124M to 760M, with supporting evidence at 1.56B and on ViT.

Appendix A Selected Hyperparameters

Table A lists the matrix-group LR and WD that each optimizer selects in the search of §5.1.

Appendix B Shampoo on GPT-2 Small

We run Shampoo [16] at small only, as the Distributed Shampoo preconditioner with exponent −1/4-1/4 per factor and no grafting, and otherwise with the recipe and tuning of the other optimizers (Table A). Shampoo lands 0.070.07 nats behind FOAM and even slightly behind AdamW (Table B), whereas SOAP, which runs Adam in the same Kronecker eigenbasis, closes this gap.

Appendix C Validity of the K-FAC Assumption

The factored update is exact under the K-FAC factorization (Lemma 1); the diagonal output side matters only for matching SOAP’s two-sided rotation (Appendix D). For each instrumented matrix we measure on checkpoints (i) the fidelity ρ⁡(W)=‖Λ−r​c⊤‖F/‖Λ‖F\rho(W)=\|\Lambda-rc^{\top}\|_{F}/\|\Lambda\|_{F}, the relative Frobenius error of the row-column factorization of the rotated second moment Λ\Lambda (ρ=0\rho=0 under K-FAC), and (ii) the sensitivity Δ⁡(W)=cos⁡(Pdense​V,HGN​V)−cos⁡(Pfac​V,HGN​V)\Delta(W)=\cos(P_{\mathrm{dense}}V,H_{\mathrm{GN}}V)-\cos(P_{\mathrm{fac}}V,H_{\mathrm{GN}}V) over random probes VV, where HGNH_{\mathrm{GN}} is the layer’s exact Gauss-Newton matrix (labels sampled from the model) and PdenseP_{\mathrm{dense}}, PfacP_{\mathrm{fac}} are FOAM’s preconditioner with the dense and the factored second moment, so that Δ\Delta isolates what the violation costs the update. The 1818 instrumented matrices are the six module types at three depths, at 124M and 350M. Table C reports every matrix at step 2,0002{,}000.

Findings.

The violation is moderate and scale-stable: ρ\rho averages 0.1620.162 at 124M and 0.1470.147 at 350M, and the row-column marginals nearly reach the best rank-one fit (rank-one energy 0.9750.975). The attention key projection is the outlier (ρ\rho up to 0.790.79 in middle and late layers; its gradients pass through RoPE and softmax), while WvW_{v} and WoW_{o} are almost exact. The consequence for the update is small: Δ\Delta averages +0.005+0.005 and +0.004+0.004, and stays below +0.05+0.05 even for WkW_{k}, consistent with the 0.0020.002-nat end-to-end difference between input-only SOAP and FOAM (Table 3). Across six training stages at 124M (steps 200200–4,7494{,}749), the 1818-matrix mean of ρ\rho stays within 0.160.16–0.190.19 and that of Δ\Delta within +0.001+0.001–+0.005+0.005, and at the three stages measured at 350M within 0.150.15–0.170.17 and +0.003+0.003–+0.004+0.004, so no stage of training makes the factored update meaningfully worse.

Appendix D Per-module Input/Output Asymmetry

Table D breaks the Gauss-Newton alignment down by module type, measured with the exact layer-wise Gauss-Newton matrix of Appendix C at step 2,0002{,}000 (Figure 5 uses a Hutchinson estimate over all 7272 matrices of a separate run). Removing the output-side rotation from the two-sided preconditioner costs 0.1600.160 of alignment on average, whereas removing the input-side rotation costs 0.3750.375; averaged over depth, input-only exceeds output-only in every module type at both scales (1.5×1.5\times to 10.9×10.9\times at 124M and 1.9×1.9\times to 11.5×11.5\times at 350M), although a few individual layers reverse the order. Output-only preconditioning (0.1320.132) is barely above diagonal Adam (0.0900.090). The two factors differ in conditioning: after normalizing each by its own diagonal, the ratio of the largest to the 2020th eigenvalue is 5.05.0 on the output side against 67.967.9 on the input side (7.47.4 against 213213 on the EMA factors SOAP maintains), so on the output side the coordinate axes already capture most of the structure.

Appendix E GPT-2 XL (1.56B)

We test whether the ordering of the three smaller sizes holds at GPT-2 XL with 1.561.56B parameters (Table E). SOAP and FOAM are tied (SOAP −- FOAM =−0.0008±0.0002=-0.0008\pm 0.0002, paired over seeds), and both are 0.0120.012–0.0130.013 nats ahead of Muon and 0.040.04 ahead of AdamW.

The model has 4848 layers and width 16001600 and otherwise follows §5.1. It is trained for 59,45059{,}450 steps of 0.50.5M tokens (3131B tokens, 1×1\times Chinchilla) on the FineWeb 100100B-token sample with 2%2\% warmup and cosine decay to 10%10\%, and evaluated on a fixed 2020M-token validation set. Each optimizer is tuned on 1111 to 1414 LR and WD cells with seed 4242, centered by the rule LR⋅WD⋅T≈const\mathrm{LR}\cdot\mathrm{WD}\cdot T\approx\text{const} fitted on the smaller sizes, and its best cell is re-run on seeds 13391339 and 20242024. SOAP and FOAM use 𝚙𝚏=10\mathtt{pf}=10.

Appendix F ViT-Tiny on Tiny-ImageNet

We test whether the comparison transfers across modality, task, and loss by training ViT-Tiny [7, 43] for Tiny-ImageNet [26] classification (Table F). The matrix-preconditioned optimizers beat AdamW (58.658.6) by 6.56.5 to 8.58.5 points of top-1 accuracy, SOAP leads (67.167.1), and FOAM is second (65.465.4), tied with Muon and AdaMuon (both 65.165.1) within noise.

We follow the plain ViT-Tiny recipe of Zhang et al. [49], with 300300 epochs, a cosine schedule with 2020-epoch warmup, and its augmentation and regularization, but train at the native image size 6464 with patch size 44 and batch 256256. Only the attention and MLP weight matrices use the optimizer under study, and all other parameters run AdamW with LR 5⋅10−45{\cdot}10^{-4} and WD 0.050.05. Each optimizer’s matrix LR and WD are tuned on a geometric grid with ratios 101/410^{1/4} and 101/210^{1/2} on one seed.

Appendix G Batch-size Scaling

A fixed token budget can be spent at different batch sizes, and under data-parallel weak scaling each batch doubling roughly halves the wall-clock time, so we test whether that speed is usable (Table G). AdamW degrades sharply (3.370→3.465→3.9563.370\to 3.465\to 3.956) and never recovers its 0.50.5M-batch quality at larger batches, whose wall-clock saving thus comes with a worse model. FOAM holds (3.309→3.315→3.3643.309\to 3.315\to 3.364) and stays ahead of Muon at every batch size, turning the same scaling into about a 3×3\times reduction in the time to AdamW’s quality (24.9→13.8→8.224.9\to 13.8\to 8.2 minutes).

GPT-2 small follows the recipe of §5.1 with a fixed 2.492.49B-token budget, i.e., 4,7504{,}750 steps at 0.50.5M tokens, and each optimizer’s LR is re-tuned at 0.50.5M, 11M, and 22M tokens per step.

Appendix H LLM Post-training

We test whether FOAM can replace AdamW in two post-training recipes on Qwen3 [45], changing only the optimizer (Table H). FOAM is best in SFT and tied with AdamW in OPD, while Muon is 0.0130.013 below both in OPD. The SFT differences among the three optimizers are within 0.0020.002 NLL, so FOAM serves as a drop-in replacement for AdamW in both recipes.

Only the 2D weight matrices of the transformer blocks use the optimizer under study, and the rest run AdamW. One LR, shared by all groups, is swept per optimizer. FOAM uses 𝚙𝚏=10\mathtt{pf}=10 and tol=0\mathrm{tol}=0, and Muon scales its update by 0.2​max⁡(m,n)0.2\sqrt{\max(m,n)}. All runs use no weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, a cosine schedule to 10%10\%, bfloat16 with fp32 master weights, and a single seed. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Qwen3-1.7B-Base is fine-tuned for one epoch on 100100K NuminaMath-CoT [27] examples (782782 steps of batch 128128, up to 4,0964{,}096 tokens, β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95)) and evaluated by the NLL on 1,0001{,}000 held-out examples. On-policy distillation (OPD) [1]. Qwen3-1.7B is distilled from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 in non-thinking mode with a per-token reverse-KL loss on its own rollouts for open reasoning prompts (100100 steps of 256256 prompts, up to 8,1928{,}192 tokens, β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999)) and scored by average accuracy on MATH500 [18, 29], AIME24, AIME25, and AMC23.
